I spent 15 years building our business from scratch, funded with my own hard-earned money, without debt or outside investment. I sold my house to finance it and put my financial security on the line. I worked evenings and weekends, went without holidays, and lived with stress that took a serious toll on my mental and physical health. There was never any guarantee that it would succeed.

Today, the business is doing very well, and we intend to sell it. The value we have created represents 15 years of work, sacrifice and personal risk. The sale is our opportunity to secure the financial future we spent those years working towards.

I accept that success comes with a tax bill. But if the government imposes a 45% tax on the gains from that sale, it crosses a line for me. Almost half the reward, after we carried the risk for 15 years, is more than I am prepared to accept. If that is the direction the UK takes, I will leave.

A government that wants people to build businesses must give them a compelling reason to build their futures here too.

The irony is that CGT applies to you as an individual (shareholder) and not to your business.  So you can leave the UK, establish your personal tax residency in a tax haven, then sell your business in the UK and pay no UK CGT at all.

There are two huge problems with this.  First it is preventing people from moving out of the UK (for example, to expand their business abroad).  Secondly and most importantly, no entrepreneurs will ever want to set up a business in the UK (and certainly not talented foreigners).  This means businesses such as Revolut (a huge UK success but built by a Russian founder) wouldnt have been established here.  If we go down this route, the UK is well and truly finished. There is a general  drift towards treating capital gain as disposable income for tax purposes. This is a fundamental strategic mistake capable of substantial economic harm. Income is short term reward for application, repeatable and not subject to much if any inflationary influence. Capital gain is mainly one off lifelong asset  growth through productivity, and some general inflation. Quite different in periodicity and origin. Capital is the seed corn for enterprise, the means to fund infrastructure schemes only capable of  the state. Reduce capital spend for current account purposes, including debt servicing,  and projects become more expensive and fewer. General decline is inevitable.

Income tax has long been held as commitment to general infrastructure, but as we know dreams of ever more elaborate  bureaucracy (EU !), and now individuals' dependence on the state, have swamped this revenue source. Debt has mounted viciously to square the circle. Now capital assets are in line for current account spend. The end point is in sight to all but the politically blind.

Small wonder betting has never been more in demand, it is the escape pod for more than half the population who have no faith in state or political promises whilst more sources of capital are being tapped to support more facing poverty of opportunity. Voters may not pay much attention to long dated bond  returns, bug they sense over exploitation of dwindling resources and diminishing hope for their kids. And as for tax evasion.....
